findings.title: SQL Injection via session-stored id bypassing LIMIT clause at high security
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php  body: id=1' OR '1'='1' #&Submit=Submit  (TRUE payload, sets session id)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (uses session-stored id, no query param)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php  body: id=1' AND '1'='2' #&Submit=Submit  (FALSE payload, sets session id)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (uses session-stored id, no query param)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Footer confirms 'Security Level: high' on all requests. TRUE payload (1' OR '1'='1' #) submitted via session-input.php then rendered on /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned ALL 5 seeded users despite the server-side query appending 'LIMIT 1' at high security -- the trailing '#' comment stripped the LIMIT clause entirely: ID: admin/admin, Gordon/Brown, Hack/Me, Pablo/Picasso, Bob/Smith (5 rows, pre_blocks confirmed each with 'ID: 1'' OR ''1''=''1'' #'). FALSE payload (1' AND '1'='2' #) submitted the same way and the subsequent GET to /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned NO result rows at all (visible_text only shows the nav chrome and 'Click here to change your ID', no ID/First name/Surname blocks, pre_blocks absent). This TRUE-multi-row vs FALSE-zero-row behavioral difference confirms exploitable out-of-band SQL injection at high security.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypassing high-security blacklist
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/  (baseline, confirms Security Level: high in footer)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe immediately followed by command, no trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist on '; ', '| ' and '&&') produced response containing pre_blocks: ['www-data'] and visible_text '...Enter an IP address: www-data More Information...'. The presence of the www-data process identity in the ping output confirms successful arbitrary OS command execution at high security.

findings.title: DVWA Stored XSS in guestbook mtxMessage field (xss_s) — security=low
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (dvwa_admin session)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After submitting the canary payload via POST (client-side maxlength attributes on txtName/mtxMessage do not restrict direct HTTP POST bodies and are bypassed), the page's HTML form summary showed a new 'Name: tester' entry was stored and rendered on the guestbook page (visible_text showed 'Name: tester Message:' with the message content rendered as executable markup rather than as escaped text, unlike the seeded 'This is a test comment.' entry which appears as plain text). Upon re-loading the page in an authenticated browser context (browser_navigate), the injected script executed: browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') confirmed the element exists in the live DOM with inner_text/inner_html 'window.xss_flag=1'. This proves the stored payload was persisted unsanitized in the database and executes as live JavaScript whenever any user views the guestbook page — confirmed stored XSS.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass (medium security) in DVWA SQLi POST form
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=medium)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Confirmed page banner shows 'Security Level: medium'. TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned ALL five seeded user records: ID:1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin; First name: Gordon Surname: Brown; First name: Hack Surname: Me; First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (no 'First name:'/'Surname:' pre_blocks present, only the empty User ID selector form). This differential behavior (multiple rows for TRUE vs zero rows for FALSE) confirms the backend concatenates the numeric id parameter directly into the SQL query without parameterization at medium security, despite mysqli_real_escape_string only protecting quote characters (bypassed via unquoted numeric injection).

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via /rest/basket/{id}
findings.response_evidence: acct1's own basket is id=6 (per session_info.own_basket_id), owned by UserId 22, containing distinct seeded item 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' qty=3 (BasketItem id=9). When authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, a different user), a direct GET to /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with the IDENTICAL basket contents belonging to UserId 22 (acct1), including the same product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' qty=3. No authorization/ownership check prevented acct2 from reading acct1's basket by ID, confirming Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA).

findings.title: Open Directory Listing Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo under /ftp/
request_sequence: GET /ftp/ (unauth, Accept: text/html,application/json) -> 200 directory listing including acquisitions.md, announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml, quarantine/
GET /ftp/acquisitions.md (unauth, no auth header) -> 200 text/markdown confidential memo content
findings.response_evidence: GET /ftp/ as unauthenticated user returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index style directory listing explicitly showing 'acquisitions.md' (909 bytes) alongside other sensitive-looking files (incident-support.kdbx, coupons_2013.md.bak, package.json.bak). Direct unauthenticated GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200 text/markdown with content: \"# Planned Acquisitions\\n\\n> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!\\n\\nOur company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.\\nThis will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail...\". This confirms the directory listing exposes the confidential document and that it is retrievable without any authentication, matching CWE-200 criteria exactly.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on /rest/user/login
findings.response_evidence: Submitting email=\"' OR 1=1--\" with an arbitrary/incorrect password (tested with two different nonsense passwords 'anything' and 'wrongpass123') both returned HTTP 200 with a valid authentication object containing a signed JWT token, bid:1 (basket id 1, matching the first/admin user), and umail:\"admin@juice-sh.op\". This confirms the SQL injection in the email field comments out the password check (\"... WHERE email='' OR 1=1--' AND password=[REDACTED]"), causing the query to match the first row in the Users table (admin) and issue a valid session token without knowing the real admin password — a full authentication bypass via SQLi.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak file extension filter in /ftp/ file server
findings.response_evidence:
Baseline: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown from fileServer.js verify() middleware (stack trace confirms extension whitelist check at /juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18).

Bypass: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200 with content_type application/octet-stream and the actual package.json file content was served, e.g.: '{
  "name": "juice-shop",
  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT",
  "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... "dependencies": { "body-parser": "~1.18", ... "sqlite3": "~3.1.13" } ...}'. This proves the null-byte truncates the path check (treats file as ending in .md), while the OS/file read uses the truncated-at-null actual filename package.json.bak, bypassing the extension whitelist filter and disclosing the restricted backup file.

findings.title: Exposed /encryptionkeys/ directory listing discloses sensitive key files (premium.key, jwt.pub)
findings.response_evidence: GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with content_type text/html; charset=utf-8 and a browsable directory listing (serve-index). Visible text: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. Links enumerated: http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the directory is browsable without authentication and exposes the sensitive JWT public key and premium feature encryption key filenames, satisfying CWE-548 exposure of sensitive information through directory listing.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection via unsanitized 'q' parameter
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote payload q=qwert') returned HTTP 500 with body: "Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error OWASP Juice Shop (Express ^4.17.1) 500 Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error" — confirming the raw input is concatenated unescaped into a SQL query (classic SQLi error signature). Request 2 (UNION-based payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- ) returned HTTP 200 with a well-formed JSON body: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} — demonstrating the attacker-controlled UNION SELECT successfully closed the injected query's parentheses/string context and returned attacker-chosen literal values (1-9) mapped directly into the product-field schema, proving successful SQL injection (not merely a search miss). Both behaviors together (SQL error on malformed quote + successful literal-value UNION injection bypassing comment) confirm CWE-89 in the product search endpoint.

findings.title: Unauthenticated User-Feedback PII Exposure via /api/Feedbacks
findings.response_evidence: Request sent with session='unauth' (no Authorization/Bearer token supplied). Response: HTTP 200, content_type application/json, body contains an array of 8 feedback records. Multiple records embed partially-masked but present author email addresses inside the free-text 'comment' field alongside a non-null UserId linking the feedback to a specific registered account, e.g.: record id=1 UserId=1 comment=\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\"; record id=2 UserId=2 comment=\"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\"; record id=3 UserId=3 comment=\"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\"; record id=4 UserId=21 comment=\"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet at /juicy-nft : \\\"purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch\\\" (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\". This endpoint requires no authentication token whatsoever yet discloses user-linked PII (partial email domains/fragments tied to specific UserId records, plus in one case what appears to be a cryptocurrency wallet seed phrase), confirming CWE-359 (unauthenticated exposure of private/sensitive user data).
